summary.text: Regression toward the mean is the phenomenon where, after one extreme sample of a random variable, the next sample is likely to be closer to its mean.
It shows up when results mix skill and luck: someone who did well may have been lucky, and luck is unlikely to repeat.
If no luck or random guessing were involved, students would score the same on a retest and there would be no regression toward the mean.

facts.label: Other names
facts.value: Regression to the mean, reversion to mediocrity

facts.label: Pure guessing case
facts.value: The retest mean falls back to the overall average

facts.label: No luck case
facts.value: Scores repeat, so there is no regression

facts.label: Sports example
facts.value: Rookie baseball hitters who hit well tend to slump in year two

items.prompt: On a 100-item true/false test, everyone guesses at random, and the top scorers then retake it, guessing again. What should you predict for their second score?

options.label: The same high score as before
Higher than before, from practice
Lower than 50, to make up for luck
About 50, the average for everyone

items.explain: Each score is pure chance with an expected mean of 50, so the best prediction for any student's second score is 50 and the group regresses all the way back.

items.prompt: Your favourite team won last year's championship, mostly thanks to luck. What does that suggest about next season?

options.label: They are more likely to win again, as champions
The more luck was behind it, the less likely a repeat
They are certain to lose, to even things out
Luck has no effect on whether a team repeats

items.explain: The greater the extent that the win was due to luck, the less likely it is that they win again next year.

items.prompt: A company has a very profitable quarter although nothing about its business has changed. What is likely next quarter?

options.label: It does better still
It does exactly the same
It does less well
It stops trading

items.explain: With the underlying reasons for performance unchanged, a highly profitable quarter is likely to be followed by a less good one.

items.prompt: Students who scored well on a test of skill plus luck sit it again. Why are they likely to do a little worse?

options.label: Some were unskilled but very lucky, and luck rarely repeats
Taking a test twice always lowers scores
Skilled students forget what they knew
The second test is always harder

items.explain: The high scorers include skilled students and unskilled ones who were extremely lucky. On a retest the unskilled are unlikely to repeat their lucky break.

items.prompt: An exam is so purely skill-based that luck and guessing play no part at all. Students sit it twice. What happens to their scores?

options.label: Scores repeat, with no regression toward the mean
Everyone regresses to the class average
The best students always fall back
The weakest students always jump to the top

items.explain: With no luck involved, all students would be expected to score the same on the second test, and there would be no regression toward the mean.

items.prompt: A class takes two editions of one test on successive days. A student with the lowest score on day one is likelier to do what on day two?

options.label: Score even lower again
Score exactly the same
Be removed from the average
Score better, since part of it was bad luck

items.explain: Scores are determined partly by ability and partly by chance, so those who were unlucky on day one tend to see their scores rise.
